lesson.title: Counting by Tens: The Decade as a Unit of Frequency Change
lesson.summary: A decade is a tenfold change in frequency, and it is the standard unit engineers use to describe how steeply a filter's response rises or falls on a logarithmic frequency scale.
lesson.body:
Frequency ranges in electronics span an enormous scale, from a few hertz for slow mechanical sensors up to gigahertz for radio and microwave signals, a span of nine orders of magnitude or more. Plotting such a range on an ordinary linear axis is nearly useless, since a graph wide enough to show 1 Hz and 1 GHz on the same linear scale would squeeze everything below a few megahertz into an unreadable sliver near the origin. Engineers solve this by plotting frequency on a logarithmic scale instead, and the natural unit for describing distances on that scale is the decade: a decade is any interval over which frequency changes by a factor of exactly 10.

Because a decade is defined multiplicatively rather than additively, the frequency range from 10 Hz to 100 Hz is one decade, and so is the range from 1000 Hz to 10000 Hz, even though the second range spans 9000 Hz while the first spans only 90 Hz. Both represent the identical proportional change, a tenfold increase, which is exactly why the logarithmic scale treats them as equal length intervals. The number of decades between any two frequencies f1 and f2 is found with a base 10 logarithm: number of decades = log10(f2 divided by f1).

Worked example: consider the range of frequencies generally audible to humans, roughly from 20 Hz up to 20000 Hz. The ratio between these two frequencies is f2/f1 = 20000/20 = 1000. The number of decades spanned is log10(1000) = 3, since 10 to the third power equals 1000 exactly. So human hearing covers exactly 3 decades of frequency, a fact that gets used directly when describing how audio equalizers or crossover filters need to perform across the full audible range. As a second check, going from 100 Hz to 1000 Hz is log10(1000/100) = log10(10) = 1 decade, confirming that a straightforward tenfold step always measures out to exactly one decade, regardless of where on the scale it starts.

Decades matter most in describing filter behavior, since a filter's attenuation slope, how fast its output falls off with frequency beyond the cutoff, is conventionally expressed in decibels per decade. A simple first order RC low pass filter, built from a single resistor and capacitor, always rolls off at 20 decibels per decade beyond its cutoff frequency, meaning that for every tenfold increase in frequency past the cutoff, the output level drops by a factor that corresponds to 20 dB, regardless of what specific resistor or capacitor values were chosen. Higher order filters, built by cascading more RC stages, roll off at steeper multiples of 20 dB per decade, giving engineers a standard vocabulary for comparing filter steepness independent of the exact component values involved.

It is worth keeping decade distinct from octave, a related but different logarithmic unit built around a factor of 2 rather than a factor of 10, which comes up constantly in audio engineering and is covered next. Both units describe proportional frequency change on a log scale, they simply use different multiplying factors as their step size.
